To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the firing rate and the firing pattern of GPi neurons are both changed by mild dyskinesia in patients with advanced PD.
the neuronal firing rate and pattern of neurons in GPi are altered in patients with mild dyskinesia resulting from low doses apomorphine.
mild dyskinesis induced by low doses apomorphine is related to decreased firing rate and altered firing pattern of neurons located in the globus palidus internus in Parkinson's disease patients.

the neuronal basis of the motor disorders of Parkinson's disease.
the neuronal basis of hyperkinesias in PD.
the neuronal mechanisms underlying hyperkinetic movement disorder.

the neuronal basis of dyskinesia is not yet fully understood.
the GPi neuronal firing pattern is altered in a complex manner in PD patients with mild dyskinesia.
the GPi firing rate is inversely related to the severity of dyskinesia, but that the relationship is more complex than this.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the GPi is a major target for pharmacological treatment of PD and that the neuronal activity of GPi neurons is altered during mild dyskinesia.
the GPi neuronal firing rate and pattern of firing are important determinants of dyskinesia in advanced PD.
low firing rates and altered neuronal firing patterns in the GPi are associated with the onset of mild dyskinesia induced by low doses apomorphine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the firing rate of neurons in the GPi is not a reliable predictor of the occurrence of dyskinesia.
dyskinesias are associated with both decreased firing rates and changes in the firing patterns of GPi neurons.
mild dyskinesis resulting from low doses apomorphine is related to both low firing rates and altered pattern of firing of the neurons of globus pallidum interna (GPi).
